sections.title: General tones
paragraphs: The regular tone categories are tones 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, and 8. Chinese originally had the four tone classes level, rising, departing, and entering, and each later split into yin and yang. Their outcomes developed differently in different regions. In commonly used Taiwanese Hokkien today, the yang rising tone has merged into the yang departing tone, so the usual inventory contains seven tones: yin level, yin rising, yin departing, yin entering, yang level, yang departing, and yang entering.

sections.title: Special tones and neutral tone
orderedItems: Some local accents preserve tone 6, as in “ǒ” (numbered form o6).
Contracted vowels and triphthongs may take tone 9 on the first vocalic segment, as in “ő” (numbered form o9).
The neutral-tone marker “--” is written between the stressed syllable and the neutral syllable. The syllable before “--” keeps its citation tone, and the syllable after it is neutral.

sections.title: Tone sandhi rules
paragraphs: Tone sandhi is a key feature of connected speech in Taiwanese Hokkien. In disyllabic words, trisyllabic words, and larger phrases, all syllables except the final one usually change according to tone-sandhi rules.
When a syllable is followed by a neutral tone, the preceding syllable keeps its citation tone and does not undergo sandhi.

sections.title: Unmarked tone notation
paragraphs: An unmarked syllable usually indicates tone 1, or follows the common dictionary and teaching convention of writing the regular reading without an added tone mark.
